nationality_or_literary_tradition: Scottish; the ballad of the city, the verse drama and the poetry of the will
literary_identity: Poet, playwright and essayist; the most original and the most neglected of the poets of the 1890s, and a forerunner of the modern poetry of the city.
biography: Born at Barrhead, Renfrewshire, on 11 April 1857, the son of a minister; he taught in Glasgow and Greenock, and went to London in 1889, where he published In a Music-Hall (1891), Fleet Street Eclogues (1893), Ballads and Songs (1894) and the 'Testaments' of the late 1890s. His verse plays were never staged successfully, his health and his marriage failed, and he drowned himself at Penzance on 23 March 1909.
literary_profile: Davidson wrote the poetry of the modern city and the modern will: In a Music-Hall and its successors are the first English poems to find a tragic art in the music hall and the street, and his long 'Testaments' are an attempt at a new secular scripture of human self-creation. His blank-verse plays and his ballads of the Scottish town are equally original, and his insistence on the poet's right to be difficult and modern made him the bridge from the 1890s to the poetry of Hardy and the Georgians.
stylistic_characteristics: The ballad and the dramatic monologue; the music-hall song and the street cry; colloquial diction and slang; long rhetorical blank verse; the 'testament' as a new form; a harsh, energetic rhythm.
intellectual_concerns: The modern city and its spectacles; the will and self-creation; poverty and the artist's degradation; Scottish town life; the loss of religious faith; the crowd and the individual.
historical_significance: Davidson is the most original poet of the 1890s and the first English poet of the modern city: his music-hall poems and his 'Testaments' anticipated the urban poetry of the twentieth century, and he is a central figure in the transition from Victorian to modern verse.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; the Catholic lyric, the ode and the poetry of the outcast
literary_identity: Poet and essayist; the author of 'The Hound of Heaven', the most famous religious poem of the English 1890s.
biography: Born at Preston on 16 December 1859, the son of a doctor; he was educated at Stonyhurst and studied medicine at Owens College, Manchester, but failed his examinations and went to London in 1885, where he lived for three years as a destitute opium addict, selling matches and sleeping on the Embankment. Wilfrid and Alice Meynell rescued him in 1888 and published his work in Merry England; Poems appeared in 1893 and Sister Songs in 1895. He died of tuberculosis at St John's Wood on 13 November 1907.
literary_profile: Thompson wrote the poetry of guilt and pursuit: 'The Hound of Heaven' is the great English poem of the soul fleeing God, and its long, irregular, tormented lines gave English religious verse a new music. His imagery is drawn from the Catholic liturgy, from the seventeenth-century poets and from the streets of London, and his essays — especially the Shelley and the 'Health and Holiness' — are among the finest of the Catholic revival.
stylistic_characteristics: Irregular odes with long, hovering lines; internal rhyme and alliteration; the imagery of blood, wings, fire and the city street; the baroque catalogue; the rhythm of the fugue.
intellectual_concerns: The pursuit of the soul by God; guilt and unworthiness; poverty and the outcast; the Eucharist and the Passion; childhood and lost innocence; London as purgatory.
historical_significance: Thompson is the finest Catholic poet of the English 1890s after Johnson and the author of the most famous religious poem of the period: 'The Hound of Heaven' reshaped English devotional poetry, and his essays and ballads made him a central figure of the Catholic literary revival.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; the dramatic monologue, the lesbian lyric and the verse of the aesthetic movement
literary_identity: Poets and diarists; the pseudonymous partnership of Katharine Bradley and her niece Edith Cooper, whose joint work is the greatest body of English love poetry written by two women.
biography: Michael Field was the pen name of Katharine Harris Bradley (1846-1914) and her niece and lover Edith Emma Cooper (1862-1913), who lived together from 1878 and wrote poems, plays and travel books as a single author. They were friends of Robert Browning, Ruskin and the Pater circle, published The Long Ago (1881), Underneath the Bough (1893) and Wild Honey from Various Thyme (1908), converted to Catholicism in 1907, and died within nine months of one another at Richmond. The rediscovery of their 9,000-page journal in the twentieth century made them central to the history of English lesbian literature.
literary_profile: Michael Field wrote the poetry of a shared life: their lyrics of love between women, written in the forms of the Elizabethan and the Celtic revival, are the most sustained English poetry of female desire in the nineteenth century. They were also considerable classical scholars, and their verse dramas and their journals are an extraordinary record of the aesthetic movement, of Victorian travel and of a lifelong partnership.
stylistic_characteristics: The sonnet sequence and the Elizabethan lyric; classical and mythological subjects; the lyric of intimacy and secrecy; the diary as a literary form; travel writing; devotional poetry after the conversion.
intellectual_concerns: Love between women and the secrecy of the shared life; classical myth and Sappho; art, poetry and the religion of beauty; travel and the European landscape; Catholic conversion and the saints; the passing of time.
historical_significance: Michael Field is the greatest and most neglected body of English love poetry written by two women: the authorship of two women in one voice, the lyrics of intimacy and the extraordinary journal have made the pair central to the recovery of Victorian women's writing and of the history of sexuality.
biographical_uncertainty: A joint pseudonym: Katharine Harris Bradley (1846-1914) and Edith Emma Cooper (1862-1913) published as one author; the birth and death dates here span the two lives.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Scottish; the chronicle novel and the literary life
literary_identity: Novelist, biographer and critic; the most prolific serious novelist of the Victorian age and the author of the Carlingford chronicles.
biography: Born Margaret Wilson at Wallyford, Midlothian, on 4 April 1828; the family moved to Liverpool and she began writing to support them. She married her cousin Frank Oliphant in 1852; he died in 1859, and she supported three children, a brother and two nieces by her pen for the rest of her life, losing two sons and a daughter. She published over a hundred books, including the Carlingford series (1861-76), Miss Marjoribanks (1866), Hester (1883) and Kirsteen (1890), wrote for Blackwood's for forty years, and died at Wimbledon on 25 June 1897.
literary_profile: Oliphant wrote the Victorian novel of the ordinary life: her subject is the woman without money, the family in decline, the provincial town and the small ambitions that make up a life, and her method is the long, easy, ironical chronicle in which nothing much happens and everything is at stake. She was also the finest woman of letters of her generation — the biographer of Edward Irving and Laurence Oliphant, the historian of the publishing house of Blackwood, and the reviewer whose essays on women, fiction and religion were read across Britain.
stylistic_characteristics: The leisurely chronicle with a large cast; free indirect style and ironic commentary; dialogue that catches provincial idiom; the comedy of the ordinary; the long view of a family across generations; a plain, flexible prose.
intellectual_concerns: Women's work and the economics of the genteel poor; marriage and the unmarried woman; provincial society and its hierarchies; family decline and inheritance; the literary profession and its costs; Scotland and the Scottish past.
historical_significance: Oliphant is the most underestimated Victorian novelist and the finest chronicler of ordinary women's lives in the century: Miss Marjoribanks and Hester are among the great English novels, her Carlingford series is the equal of Trollope's Barsetshire, and her autobiography is one of the most moving documents of Victorian literary life.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; the domestic chronicle and the High Church novel
literary_identity: Novelist and historian; the most influential writer of the Victorian High Church novel and the inventor of the family chronicle for girls.
biography: Born Charlotte Mary Yonge at Otterbourne, Hampshire, on 11 August 1823, the daughter of a retired army officer; she was educated at home and never married, living all her life in the village where her father was patron of the living. Her first novel appeared in 1844, and The Heir of Redclyffe (1853) made her famous; she edited The Monthly Packet for nearly forty years and wrote over a hundred and fifty books, including the sequence of family chronicles known as the 'Dynasty'. She died at Otterbourne on 24 May 1901.
literary_profile: Yonge wrote the novel of church and family: her subject is the moral formation of a young person within the discipline of the family and the Anglican communion, and her enormous 'Dynasty' follows a group of intermarried families through the nineteenth century. She was more influential on the Victorian imagination than any novelist except Dickens — The Heir of Redclyffe was the favourite book of the young officers of the Crimean War — and her best work is a fine, dense picture of the ordinary life of the Victorian gentry.
stylistic_characteristics: The large family chronicle with an enormous cast; the direct moral appeal; dialogue of the county and the vicarage; the historical novel of the English church; the deathbed scene; the use of the novel for teaching.
intellectual_concerns: Religious faith and church loyalty; the family and its moral discipline; the education of children; the history of the Church of England; class and the county gentry; renunciation and self-sacrifice.
historical_significance: Yonge was the most influential woman novelist of the mid-Victorian period and the founder of the family chronicle for girls: The Heir of Redclyffe shaped the Victorian ideal of the Christian gentleman, her historical novels taught a generation its church history, and her 'Dynasty' is one of the most ambitious fictional projects of the century.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; the domestic novel, the children's book and the woman's career
literary_identity: Novelist, poet and essayist; the author of John Halifax, Gentleman and one of the most successful self-supporting women writers of the century.
biography: Born Dinah Maria Mulock at Hartshill, Staffordshire, on 20 April 1826, the daughter of a Dissenting minister; after her father's death she moved to London in 1846 and supported herself and her brothers by her pen. John Halifax, Gentleman (1856) made her famous; she married the publisher George Lillie Craik in 1865 and wrote over thirty books, including the children's classic The Little Lame Prince. She died at Shortlands, Kent, on 12 October 1887.
literary_profile: Craik wrote the Victorian novel of the self-made man and the self-supporting woman: John Halifax is the classic Victorian story of the poor boy who becomes a great manufacturer, and A Woman's Thoughts about Women is the most practical of Victorian essays on the single woman's life. Her children's books are among the finest of the 1870s, and her best fiction unites sentiment with a firm grasp of money and work.
stylistic_characteristics: Plain, warm narrative prose; the exemplary life told in episodes; domestic detail and the comedy of the household; sentimental climax; the essay of practical advice; simple allegory for children.
intellectual_concerns: The making of a fortune and the ethics of business; self-help and the working life; marriage and the unmarried woman; poverty and respectability; childhood and disability; Christian duty in the world.
historical_significance: Craik was one of the most widely read novelists of the 1850s-70s: John Halifax, Gentleman was the classic Victorian book of self-help, A Woman's Thoughts about Women was a formative text for the single woman of the period, and The Little Lame Prince is a permanent children's classic.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; the periodical essay, the novel of the woman question and the satirical sketch
literary_identity: Novelist and journalist; the first woman to earn a regular salary on the London press, and the most notorious 'anti-feminist' essayist of the Victorian age.
biography: Born Eliza Lynn at Keswick on 10 February 1822, the daughter of a clergyman; she went to London in 1845 and became the first woman employed on the staff of a London daily newspaper, the Morning Chronicle. She married the wood-engraver William Linton in 1858 and left him in 1867; she published twenty-five novels and a mass of journalism, and her essay 'The Girl of the Period' (1868) made her the most discussed woman writer in England after George Eliot. She died in London on 14 July 1898.
literary_profile: Linton wrote the essay that named the modern young woman: 'The Girl of the Period' is a satire on the fashionable girl who paints her face and thinks of nothing but dress, and it set the terms of the debate on the New Woman for twenty years. But her position was more complex than the label 'anti-feminist' allows: her novels attack the marriage law, her journalism defends women's right to work, and her autobiography is one of the frankest records of a woman's professional life in the century.
stylistic_characteristics: The satirical periodical essay with a strong persona; the social sketch; the novel of the woman question with a harsh realism about money and sex; the ironic description of dress and manners; direct polemical address.
intellectual_concerns: The 'woman question' and the modern girl; marriage, work and female independence; dress, fashion and the body; class and the professions; the condition of women in the colonies; the vanity of the fashionable world.
historical_significance: Linton is the central figure in the Victorian debate on the 'Girl of the Period' and one of the first women to hold a salaried post on the London press: her journalism set the terms of the debate over the New Woman, and her autobiography and her best novels are key documents of Victorian women's professional life.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; the novel of faith and the social-problem novel
literary_identity: Novelist; the best-selling serious novelist of the 1880s-1900s and the author of Robert Elsmere, the central Victorian novel of the loss of faith.
biography: Born Mary Augusta Arnold at Hobart, Tasmania, on 11 June 1851, the granddaughter of Thomas Arnold and niece of Matthew Arnold; the family returned to England in 1856 and she was educated at Oxford and in London. She married the historian Thomas Humphry Ward in 1872, wrote for the Times and Macmillan's, and published Robert Elsmere in 1888; she founded the Passmore Edwards Settlement in 1897 and worked for women's education. She led the anti-suffrage movement from 1908 and died in London on 24 March 1920.
literary_profile: Ward wrote the novel of the Victorian crisis of faith: Robert Elsmere is the book in which the Broad Church conscience, the higher criticism and the social gospel meet, and its account of a clergyman who loses his belief and finds a religion of social service was the most discussed English novel of the decade. Her later novels — Marcella, Sir George Tressady, Helbeck of Bannisdale — treat the woman question, politics and Catholicism with the same seriousness, and her biography of her father is a fine piece of Victorian life-writing.
stylistic_characteristics: The long novel of ideas with a large social canvas; dialogue that argues a theological or political case; the domestic interior as the stage of moral crisis; the set-piece description of a landscape or an institution; a plain and dignified prose.
intellectual_concerns: Religious doubt and the social gospel; the Broad Church and the higher criticism; the woman question and women's education; politics and the political conscience; Catholicism and the modern world; the university and the settlement house.
historical_significance: Ward was the most widely read serious novelist of her generation and Robert Elsmere the central English novel of the Victorian religious crisis: it sold in hundreds of thousands and was discussed from every pulpit, and its picture of the transition from faith to social service made it the representative novel of the 1880s.
